corrections.reason: Clarify that the answer selects partitioning and mount identification rather than a complete disk-preparation runbook.
corrections.actualSourceClaim: The retained Linux attach-disk article requires GPT for disks at least 2 TiB, shows mkfs filesystem creation, and recommends filesystem UUID for /etc/fstab.

before.scenario: A new, empty 3-TiB managed data disk is attached to a Linux VM. It must be partitioned and mounted persistently; the operator has verified the disk identity and confirmed there is no data to preserve.
before.prompt: Which preparation meets the documented requirements?

options.text: Use GPT partitioning and identify the filesystem by UUID in /etc/fstab
options.explanation: The Linux attach-disk guidance requires GPT for disks at least 2 TiB and recommends UUIDs rather than device names for persistent mount entries.

options.text: Use only MBR partitioning and identify the mount permanently as /dev/sdc1
options.explanation: The guidance requires GPT at this disk size and warns that device names can refer to another disk after detection-order changes.

options.text: Skip filesystem preparation because attaching a new blank disk creates the filesystem automatically
options.explanation: The attach-disk procedure still requires partitioning and formatting a new disk before mounting it in the guest.

before.summaryExplanation: The Linux attach-disk guidance requires GPT for disks at least 2 TiB and recommends UUIDs rather than device names for persistent mount entries.

references.title: Use the portal to attach a data disk to a Linux VM - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn
references.evidenceSummary: Actual retrieved Microsoft Learn excerpt: of parted that's available for your distribution. If the disk size is 2 tebibytes (TiB) or larger, you must use GPT partitioning. If disk size is under 2 TiB, then you can use either MBR or GPT partitioning. SCSI NVMe The following example uses parted on /dev/sdc , which is where the first data disk typically is on most VMs. Replace sdc with the correct option for your disk. The example formats the partition by using the XFS file system. sudo parted /dev/sdc --script mklabel gpt mkpart xfspart xf |  the drive is automatically added after a reboot. Ensure that the UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is used in /etc/fstab to refer to the drive rather than a device name, such as /dev/sdc1 or /dev/nvme0n2p1 . If the OS detects a disk error during boot, using the UUID avoids the incorrect disk being mounted to a given location. Remaining data disks would then be assigned those same device IDs. To find the UUID of the new drive, use the blkid utility. sudo blkid The following output i Scenario interpretation: The Linux attach-disk guidance requires GPT for disks at least 2 TiB and recommends UUIDs rather than device names for persistent mount entries.

corrections.reason: Make the authorised HTTP rollout assumption explicit; this narrows the scenario rather than proving TCP cannot split traffic.
corrections.actualSourceClaim: The retained Container Apps revisions article supports multiple active revisions and traffic splitting in multiple revision mode. Its traffic-splitting example explicitly presumes enabled ingress and says HTTP or TCP; the clarification selects HTTP and does not claim TCP is unsupported.

before.scenario: A team runs Container Apps in multiple revision mode during a gradual application update. It wants to send some traffic to a newer revision while retaining an older active revision.
before.prompt: Which TWO concepts support this rollout?

options.text: A revision is an immutable snapshot of a version of the container app
options.explanation: The revision model represents an immutable version snapshot, allowing the operator to identify which app version each active revision runs.

options.text: Every new revision immediately destroys all existing revisions in multiple revision mode
options.explanation: Multiple revision mode allows several revisions to remain active; creation does not itself require deleting every existing revision.

options.text: Multiple revision mode can split traffic between active revisions
options.explanation: The revisions documentation describes traffic splitting across active revisions as a multiple-revision capability.

options.text: Replica count is a replacement for choosing which revision receives traffic
options.explanation: Replicas scale within a revision, while traffic allocation determines which revision serves the request; these are separate controls.

before.summaryExplanation: The revision model represents an immutable version snapshot, allowing the operator to identify which app version each active revision runs. The revisions documentation describes traffic splitting across active revisions as a multiple-revision capability.

references.evidenceSummary: Actual retrieved Microsoft Learn excerpt: er app. Key characteristics of revisions include: Immutable : Once established, a revision remains unchangeable. Versioned : Revisions act as a record of the container app's versions, capturing its state at various stages. Automatically provisioned : When you deploy a container app for the first time, an initial revision is automatically created. Scoped changes : While revisions remain static, application-scope changes can affect all revisions, while revision-scope changes create a new revisio |  revisions, and simplified rollbacks. No Multiple You can have multiple active revisions, split traffic between revisions, and choose when to deprovision old revisions. This level of control is helpful for testing multiple versions of an app, blue-green testing, or taking full control of app updates. Refer to traffic splitting for more detail.
